prompt: Pull requests are assigned one per reviewer, and nobody may review their own. Why is subtracting one self-review count per engineer from all permutations insufficient?

options.text: Assignments with several self-reviews are subtracted more than once.
options.explanation: The forbidden events overlap and need inclusion–exclusion.

options.text: A reviewer may receive arbitrarily many requests.
options.explanation: The assignment is a permutation, one request per reviewer.
A permutation can contain fixed points, including the identity assignment.
Several engineers can receive their own requests in one assignment.

workedExample: An assignment in which Alice and Ben both self-review belongs to two forbidden groups. Subtracting both removes it twice, although it needs removal only once. Add pairwise overlaps back and continue correcting higher overlaps. A derangement is what remains after excluding every fixed point.

prompt: Five distinct jobs must be assigned to three distinct servers, all used. Why does ordinary stars and bars on the three job counts fail to count these assignments?

options.explanation: Ordinary stars and bars does allow empty bins; lower bounds can also be handled.

options.text: It forgets which particular jobs each server receives.
options.explanation: Different assignments can have identical counts per server.

options.text: The servers must all receive equal counts.
options.explanation: The only requirement is at least one each.

options.text: The jobs must run in a specified order.
options.explanation: The question assigns jobs to servers, without specifying execution order.

workedExample: Compare giving Alice’s job or Ben’s job to the first server while preserving each server’s total. Those are different assignments because jobs are distinct. A count-only distribution loses that distinction. Count functions from jobs to servers and exclude assignments missing a server, correcting overlapping exclusions.
